title: Difference Between Metro and RRTS: Complete Comparison 2026
description: Metro vs RRTS explained in detail: speed, stations, coaches, fare, technology and purpose compared, with Delhi Metro and Namo Bharat as real examples.
body:
If you have travelled on both Delhi Metro and Namo Bharat, you already know they feel different, even though both run on elevated tracks, use similar looking trains, and get you around the National Capital Region. But metro and RRTS are actually two different categories of transit systems, built for two different jobs. Understanding the difference between metro and RRTS makes it much easier to choose the right one for your journey and to understand why one costs more, stops less, and moves faster than the other.

This guide breaks down the difference between metro and RRTS point by point, using [Delhi Metro](https://metroguideindia.com/delhi-metro/) and [Namo Bharat](https://metroguideindia.com/namo-bharat/) as real, current examples.

## What Is RRTS? A Quick Definition

**RRTS stands for Regional Rapid Transit System.** It is a rail-based transit system designed to connect an entire city to nearby cities or regions at high speed, with very few stops along the way. In India, RRTS trains are branded as **Namo Bharat**, and the first operational corridor connects Delhi to Meerut across 82.15 km in under an hour.

RRTS is not a replacement for metro. It works alongside metro systems, handling the longer, intercity portion of a commute while metro handles the shorter, intracity portion.

## What Is Metro? A Quick Definition

A **metro rail system** is an urban rail network designed to move people around within a single city. Stations are spaced closely together, usually one to two kilometres apart, so that most neighbourhoods have a station within walking distance. [Delhi Metro](https://metroguideindia.com/delhi-metro/), with its Red, Blue, Yellow, Pink, and other lines, is the most well-known example in North India, along with systems like Namma Metro in Bengaluru and Chennai Metro.

Metro systems prioritise coverage and accessibility within a city, which naturally means more stops and a lower average speed compared to RRTS.

## Metro vs RRTS: Quick Comparison Table

| Feature | Metro (e.g. Delhi Metro) | RRTS (Namo Bharat) |
| Purpose | Intracity travel, within one city | Intercity travel, connecting cities/regions |
| Station spacing | Close together, 1 to 2 km apart | Wide apart, 5 to 10 km apart |
| Operating speed | Up to 80 to 90 km/h, average speed lower due to frequent stops | Up to 160 km/h operational |
| Design speed | Around 90 to 95 km/h | 180 km/h |
| Average journey speed | Approximately 32 to 34 km/h including stops | Approximately 80 to 90 km/h including stops |
| Coach layout | Longitudinal seating, standing space prioritised | Aircraft-style forward facing seating, more legroom |
| Number of coaches | Typically 6 to 8 coaches | 6 coaches, including 1 Premium coach |
| Classes | Single class | Standard Class and Premium Class |
| Frequency | 2 to 5 minutes at peak hours | 5 to 15 minutes |
| Fare structure | Distance based, generally lower | Distance based, generally higher for comparable distance |
| Signalling | CBTC (Communication Based Train Control) | ETCS Level 2 European signalling standard |
| Examples in India | Delhi Metro, Namma Metro, Chennai Metro | Namo Bharat (Delhi–Meerut, with Delhi–Alwar and Delhi–Panipat under construction) |

## Speed: The Biggest Practical Difference

This is usually the first thing commuters notice. Delhi Metro trains have a design speed of around 90 to 95 km/h, but because stations come every kilometre or two, the actual average speed including stops works out closer to 32 to 34 km/h.

Namo Bharat trains run at an operational speed of up to 160 km/h, with a design speed of 180 km/h. Because stations are spaced much further apart, roughly every 5 to 10 km, the train spends more time at top speed and less time stopping, which is why the Delhi to Meerut journey takes under an hour despite covering 82 km.

In short: metro is fast between two nearby points, RRTS is fast across long distances.

## Station Spacing and Coverage

Metro systems are built for coverage. Delhi Metro alone has over 250 stations across its network, packed closely enough that most residents in the city are within walking or short auto-rickshaw distance of one.

RRTS is built for connection, not coverage. Namo Bharat's Delhi–Meerut corridor has just 22 stations across 82 km, which works out to a station roughly every 3.5 to 4 km on average, and considerably more in less dense stretches. This wider spacing is exactly what allows RRTS trains to maintain high speed, since fewer stops mean less time spent accelerating and decelerating.

## Coach Design and Comfort

Step inside a Namo Bharat train and the difference from a metro coach is immediately obvious. Namo Bharat uses aircraft-style forward and backward facing seating with more legroom, overhead luggage racks, and a noticeably quieter ride, since it is designed for commuters travelling 30 to 80 km at a stretch, not a five minute hop.

Delhi Metro coaches use longitudinal seating along the walls, prioritising standing space to move a larger number of passengers over shorter distances during rush hour. This makes sense for a system where the average trip is short and frequent, but it would be uncomfortable for an hour long journey, which is exactly the gap RRTS was designed to fill.

Namo Bharat also offers a **Premium Class coach**, roughly 20% costlier than Standard, with extra comfort features. Delhi Metro does not have a separate premium class, since journeys are shorter and the pricing model does not need that tier.

## Fare Comparison

Because RRTS covers longer distances at higher speed with more comfortable coaches, its fares are naturally higher than metro for a comparable distance. Namo Bharat's Standard Class fares on the Delhi–Meerut corridor range from approximately ₹20 to ₹210 depending on distance, while Delhi Metro fares for a comparable trip length are generally lower, since metro fares are structured around shorter average journeys.

For the exact fare on the Namo Bharat network between any two stations, use the live [fare calculator on MetroGuideIndia](https://metroguideindia.com/fares) rather than relying on a static number, since it reflects current NCRTC pricing.

## Technology and Signalling

Both systems are modern, but RRTS uses a more advanced signalling standard suited to its higher speeds. Namo Bharat runs on **ETCS Level 2**, a European Train Control System standard that allows safe, high-frequency operation at high speed by continuously communicating train position and speed data between the train and the control centre.

Delhi Metro primarily uses **CBTC (Communication Based Train Control)**, which is well suited to metro's shorter distances and closer station spacing, allowing trains to run at tighter intervals within the city.

Both systems use platform screen doors at stations for passenger safety, and both are fully air-conditioned.

## Frequency and Waiting Time

Metro systems generally run more frequently because they carry far more daily riders across shorter hops. Delhi Metro trains can arrive every 2 to 5 minutes during peak hours on busy lines.

Namo Bharat trains run every 10 to 15 minutes, based on the current schedule and expected demand for the Delhi–Meerut corridor. This is expected to improve as ridership grows and more rolling stock is added to the corridor. Check the [Namo Bharat timings page](https://metroguideindia.com/timings) for the latest frequency updates.

## Which One Should You Choose?

The honest answer is that metro and RRTS are not competing options, they are complementary. If you are travelling within Delhi, say from Rajiv Chowk to Dwarka, Delhi Metro is the obvious choice, since RRTS does not stop at most intracity locations.

If you are travelling from Delhi to Ghaziabad or Meerut, Namo Bharat is significantly faster and more comfortable than either the metro or road travel, even though it costs more per kilometre.

Many commuters actually use both in the same trip. For example, someone living near Rajiv Chowk who works in Meerut might take Delhi Metro to Anand Vihar, then switch to Namo Bharat for the rest of the journey, since both systems interchange directly at several stations including Anand Vihar, Sarai Kale Khan, New Ashok Nagar, and Sahibabad.

For the full station-by-station breakdown of where these interchanges happen, along with the complete route, timings, and fare details, see our complete [**Namo Bharat RRTS Guide 2026**](https://metroguideindia.com/blog/namo-bharat-rrts-guide-2026-routes-stations-timings-fare-complete-travel-guide).

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What does RRTS stand for?** RRTS stands for Regional Rapid Transit System, a rail network designed to connect cities and regions at high speed with fewer stops than a metro.

**Is Namo Bharat a metro?** No. Namo Bharat is an RRTS, not a metro. It is faster, has fewer and more widely spaced stations, and is designed for intercity travel rather than travel within a single city.

**What is the main difference between metro and RRTS?** Metro is built for frequent stops and short trips within a city, while RRTS is built for high speed travel between cities with far fewer stops. Namo Bharat runs up to 160 km/h, compared to an average speed of around 32 to 34 km/h for Delhi Metro including stops.

**Is RRTS more expensive than metro?** Yes, generally. RRTS fares are higher than metro fares for a comparable distance, reflecting the higher speed, more comfortable coaches, and Premium Class option available on Namo Bharat.

**Can I use the same ticket for metro and RRTS?** Currently, Namo Bharat and Delhi Metro use separate ticketing systems, though the RRTS Connect app supports DMRC ticket booking as part of the One India, One Ticket initiative, making it easier to plan a combined journey.

**Which is faster, Delhi Metro or Namo Bharat?** Namo Bharat is significantly faster over long distances, with an operational speed of up to 160 km/h compared to Delhi Metro's average speed of around 32 to 34 km/h including stops. Over very short distances within a single neighbourhood, metro can feel just as quick since RRTS stations are far more spread out.
